title: Linux Text Processing: grep, sed, awk & the Pipeline
summary: A dense field guide to the classic Unix text-processing toolchain — regular expressions, grep searching, sed stream editing, awk field programs, and cut/sort/uniq — plus how to chain them into pipelines that solve real log, CSV, and data-munging problems. Covers mechanics, locale and performance trade-offs, and the gotchas that silently corrupt results.

chapters.title: The Filter Model: Lines, Streams, Pipes
points: Unix text tools are filters: read stdin (or file args), write stdout, errors to stderr — this uniform contract is what makes chaining possible
A 'text file' is a byte stream split on \n; POSIX says a line ends with \n, so a file whose last line lacks it is technically malformed (many tools still process it, some drop it)
`cmd1 | cmd2` connects cmd1's stdout to cmd2's stdin via a kernel pipe buffer (typically 64 KB on Linux); both processes run concurrently, not sequentially
Streaming means constant memory: `grep ERROR huge.log` works on a 500 GB file because it holds one line at a time, unlike loading into an editor
Exit status is the second output channel: 0 = success/match found, 1 = no match, >1 = error. `grep -q pat file && echo yes` is the idiom
Buffering trap: stdout is line-buffered to a TTY but block-buffered (4–8 KB) into a pipe, so `tail -f log | grep X | tee out` stalls; fix with `grep --line-buffered` or `stdbuf -oL`
Redirection vs pipe: `>` writes to a file, `|` writes to a process. `cmd > file` truncates the file *before* cmd runs, so `sort f > f` destroys f
In-place editing is not native to filters: use `sed -i`, or `cmd f > tmp && mv tmp f`, or `sponge` from moreutils
`-` as a filename means stdin for most tools: `cat header.txt - < body.txt`
Broken pipe: `yes | head -1` makes `yes` receive SIGPIPE and die — this is the mechanism that lets infinite producers work in pipelines
Tool division of labor: grep selects lines, sed edits lines, awk computes on fields, cut slices columns, sort orders, uniq collapses adjacent duplicates

chapters.title: Regular Expressions I: BRE, ERE, and the Escaping Trap
points: Three dialects matter: POSIX Basic (BRE — grep, sed default), POSIX Extended (ERE — grep -E, sed -E, awk), and PCRE (grep -P, Perl/Python)
In BRE, `+ ? { } | ( )` are LITERAL characters; you must backslash them: `\+ \? \{ \} \| \( \)`. In ERE they are metacharacters and backslashing makes them literal — exactly inverted
Core atoms: `.` any char except newline, `[abc]` class, `[^abc]` negated class, `[a-z]` range, `\.` literal dot
Anchors: `^` start of line, `$` end of line. `^$` matches an empty line. `^` is only special at the start of a BRE, literal elsewhere
Quantifiers: `*` 0+, `+` 1+ (ERE), `?` 0 or 1 (ERE), `{n}` exactly n, `{n,m}` n to m, `{n,}` n or more
Alternation: ERE `cat|dog`, BRE `cat\|dog` (GNU extension; not in strict POSIX BRE)
Grouping and backreferences: `\(ab\)\1` in BRE, `(ab)\1` in ERE — backreferences make matching non-regular and potentially exponential
POSIX bracket classes work inside `[]` and are locale-aware: `[[:digit:]] [[:alpha:]] [[:space:]] [[:alnum:]] [[:punct:]] [[:upper:]]`
Inside `[]`, most metacharacters lose power: `[.*+]` matches literal dot, star, plus. To include `]` put it first `[]a]`; to include `-` put it last `[a-]`; `^` first negates
GNU word boundaries: `\b` boundary, `\<` `\>` word start/end, `\w` = `[[:alnum:]_]`, `\s` whitespace — GNU extensions, not portable to BSD/macOS
Greediness: POSIX regex is leftmost-longest. `<.*>` on `<a><b>` matches the whole string, not `<a>`. Fix with a negated class `<[^>]*>` (works everywhere) rather than lazy `.*?` (PCRE only)
Always single-quote patterns in the shell: `grep '$foo\|bar'` — double quotes let the shell eat `$`, `` ` ``, and `\`

chapters.title: grep: Search Mechanics and Core Flags
points: grep prints every input line matching a pattern; the name comes from the ed command `g/re/p` (globally, regular expression, print)
Variants are one binary with flags: `grep` = BRE, `grep -E`/egrep = ERE, `grep -F`/fgrep = fixed strings (no regex, uses Aho–Corasick, fastest), `grep -P` = PCRE
`-i` case-insensitive, `-v` invert (print non-matching), `-w` whole word, `-x` whole line, `-c` count matching lines (not matches), `-n` line numbers
`-o` prints only the matched part, one per line — this is how you turn grep into an extractor: `grep -o '[0-9]\{1,3\}\.[0-9...]' access.log`
`-l` lists filenames with a match, `-L` lists files WITHOUT a match, `-h` suppress filename prefix, `-H` force it
`-q` quiet: exits at the first match with status 0 and prints nothing — use in `if` conditions, never with a pipe you need output from
`-e pat` allows multiple patterns and patterns starting with `-`; `-f file` reads one pattern per line from a file
`-F -f wordlist.txt` is the fast way to match thousands of fixed strings at once — a regex alternation of 10k terms is far slower
`-c` counts LINES, not occurrences. To count occurrences use `grep -o pat f | wc -l`
`grep -v` inverting a multi-condition pattern is not the negation you expect: `grep -v 'a\|b'` drops lines with a OR b (De Morgan applies)
Return codes: 0 match, 1 no match, 2 file error — so `grep pat missing.txt; echo $?` prints 2, and `set -e` scripts die on an honest no-match
Binary files: grep prints 'Binary file X matches' and stops; force with `-a`/`--text`, skip with `-I`

chapters.title: grep at Scale: Context, Recursion, and PCRE
points: Context flags: `-A n` after, `-B n` before, `-C n` both. Non-adjacent groups are separated by `--`; suppress with `--no-group-separator`
`-r` recursive from a directory, `-R` also follows symlinks. `grep -rn 'TODO' src/` is the daily driver
`--include='*.py'` / `--exclude='*.min.js'` / `--exclude-dir=.git` filter the recursive walk — far cheaper than piping through `find`
`grep -P` unlocks lazy quantifiers `.*?`, lookahead `(?=...)`, lookbehind `(?<=...)`, `\d \w \s`, and `\K` to drop everything matched so far
`\K` extraction idiom: `grep -oP 'user=\K\w+'` prints just the username, no capture-group post-processing needed
Lookahead AND-logic: `grep -P '(?=.*error)(?=.*timeout)'` matches lines containing both terms in any order — impossible in one plain ERE
`grep -z` treats input as NUL-separated records, enabling multi-line matching: `grep -Pzo '(?s)BEGIN.*?END'`
`-m n` stops after n matching lines — huge win on big files when you only need a sample
Filename-safe piping: `grep -rlZ pat . | xargs -0 sed -i 's/a/b/g'` — `-Z`/`-0` handle spaces and newlines in names
Performance ladder: `-F` (fixed) < BRE/ERE (DFA, linear time) < `-P` (backtracking NFA, can blow up). Prefer the weakest tool that works
GNU grep is fast because it uses Boyer–Moore to skip bytes and avoids splitting lines it can prove cannot match; `LC_ALL=C grep` skips UTF-8 decoding and is often 2–10x faster on ASCII data
Modern alternatives (`ripgrep`, `ag`) default to recursive, gitignore-aware, PCRE-ish search — but grep is the one guaranteed present on every box

chapters.title: sed: The Stream Editor Execution Cycle
points: sed is a line-oriented programmable editor: it reads a line into the pattern space, runs the whole script against it, auto-prints the pattern space, then repeats
The cycle is the mental model — every command is 'do X to the current pattern space', and understanding auto-print explains most sed confusion
`-n` suppresses auto-print; then `p` prints explicitly. `sed -n '5p'` prints line 5; without `-n` it prints line 5 twice
Script structure: `[address[,address]]command[arguments]`. No address = every line
Addresses: `5` line 5, `$` last line, `/re/` matching lines, `5,10` range, `/start/,/end/` regex range, `0~3` every 3rd line (GNU), `5,+2` line 5 and 2 after
`!` negates an address: `sed '/^#/!d'` deletes everything that is NOT a comment
Multiple commands: `-e 'cmd1' -e 'cmd2'`, or semicolons `'cmd1;cmd2'`, or braces for grouped addressing `'/re/{s/a/b/;d}'`
`-f script.sed` runs a script file; `-i` edits in place (`-i.bak` keeps a backup — required syntax on BSD/macOS, where bare `-i` needs an explicit `''`)
`-E` (or `-r` in older GNU) switches to ERE so you drop the `\(` `\{` `\|` backslashes
The hold space is a second buffer: `h` copy pattern→hold, `H` append, `g` hold→pattern, `G` append, `x` exchange. `sed '1!G;h;$!d'` reverses a file (a tac implementation)
`N` appends the next line into the pattern space (with an embedded \n) enabling two-line matches; `D`/`P` operate on the first embedded line for sliding windows
sed is Turing-complete via hold space, branching (`b`, `t`, `:label`), but anything needing that is a job for awk or a real language

chapters.title: sed Substitution: s/// in Full Detail
points: Form: `s/regex/replacement/flags`. Replaces the FIRST match on each line by default
The delimiter is whatever follows `s` — use `s|/usr/bin|/opt/bin|` or `s#...#...#` to avoid escaping slashes in paths

Flag `g` = all matches on the line; `Ng` = from the Nth match onward; `N` alone = only the Nth match; `i`/`I` = case-insensitive; `p` = print (pairs with `-n`); `w file` = write matched lines to a file
`&` in the replacement means 'the entire match': `sed 's/[0-9]\+/[&]/g'` brackets every number
Capture groups: `\(...\)` in BRE / `(...)` with `-E`, referenced as `\1`..`\9` in the replacement — `sed -E 's/(\w+) (\w+)/\2 \1/'` swaps two words
GNU case conversion in the replacement: `\U` upper until `\E`, `\L` lower, `\u`/`\l` next char only — `sed 's/.*/\u&/'` capitalizes each line
Escaping newlines: `\n` in a replacement inserts a newline (GNU); to match one you must first get two lines into the pattern space with `N`
Delete/insert/append/change: `d` delete, `i\text` insert before, `a\text` append after, `c\text` replace the line, `r file` read a file in, `q` quit (`sed '100q'` ≈ `head -100` and stops reading)
`y/abc/xyz/` is transliteration — a character-by-character map, sed's `tr`
Idioms: strip trailing whitespace `sed 's/[[:space:]]*$//'`; delete blank lines `sed '/^$/d'`; strip comments `sed 's/#.*//'`; print a range `sed -n '10,20p'`
Untrusted input in the pattern is a real hazard — a variable containing `/` or `&` breaks or rewrites the command; sanitize or use awk instead
`s///` operates on the pattern space, so it cannot see across lines unless you built a multi-line pattern space with `N`

chapters.title: cut and tr: Cheap Column Slicing
points: `cut` extracts sections of each line by byte (`-b`), character (`-c`), or field (`-f`)
`cut -d: -f1,3 /etc/passwd` — `-d` sets a single-CHARACTER delimiter; multi-char delimiters are not supported (that is awk's job)
Field lists accept ranges: `-f2-4`, `-f3-` (3 to end), `-f-3` (start to 3), and comma lists `-f1,5,9`
cut always outputs fields in FILE order, never the order you listed: `cut -f3,1` prints field 1 then 3. Reordering requires awk
`--output-delimiter=X` changes the output separator; without it the input delimiter is reused
`-s` suppresses lines lacking the delimiter; by default such lines are printed whole, which silently pollutes output

cut does NOT collapse repeated delimiters: two adjacent spaces make an empty field, so `cut -d' '` on space-aligned output is almost always wrong — use `awk '{print $2}'` or pre-squeeze with `tr -s ' '`
cut has no quoting awareness, so it cannot parse real CSV with embedded commas inside quotes — use a CSV-aware tool (`csvcut`, python) there
`tr` translates or deletes characters and reads only stdin (no file args): `tr 'a-z' 'A-Z'`, `tr -d '\r'` (strip CRLF), `tr -s ' '` (squeeze runs), `tr -cd '[:print:]'` (keep printable only)
`tr '\n' ' '` joins lines; `tr ' ' '\n'` splits into one word per line — the standard prelude to `sort | uniq -c`
Speed: cut and tr are the cheapest tools here — no regex engine at all. On multi-GB files, `cut -f1` beats `awk '{print $1}'` measurably
`paste` is cut's inverse: `paste -d, a.txt b.txt` joins files column-wise; `paste -sd,` folds lines into one comma-joined line

chapters.title: sort: Keys, Ordering, and Correctness
points: `sort` orders lines; with no options it does a full-line comparison in the current locale's collation order
`-n` numeric sort, `-g` general numeric (handles 1e5 and inf, slower), `-h` human-readable (2K < 3M < 1G), `-V` version sort (v1.9 < v1.10)
`-r` reverse, `-u` unique (dedupe by the SORT KEY, not the whole line — a subtle difference from `uniq`)
`-k` selects key fields: `-k2,2` sorts by field 2 ONLY. Writing `-k2` means 'from field 2 to end of line', a very common bug
Per-key modifiers attach to the key: `sort -k3,3n -k1,1r` sorts numerically by field 3, then reverse-alphabetically by field 1
`-t` sets the field separator; without it fields are whitespace-runs and leading blanks are part of the field (use `-b` or the `b` key modifier to skip them)
sort is NOT stable by default — equal keys may be reordered. `-s` forces stability, which matters when chaining multiple sorts
Locale bites: in `en_US.UTF-8`, sort ignores punctuation and case in collation, so results differ from ASCII order. `LC_ALL=C sort` gives byte order, is deterministic, and is much faster
sort must buffer to order, so it is the memory/latency wall in a streaming pipeline: it cannot emit anything until it has read everything
Complexity is O(n log n); GNU sort spills to temp files (`-T dir`) for inputs larger than RAM (external merge sort) and parallelizes with `--parallel=N`, `-S 2G` sets the buffer
`-m` merges already-sorted files in O(n) — never re-sort what is already sorted
`-c` checks sortedness without output; `-z` handles NUL-terminated records from `find -print0`

chapters.title: uniq: Adjacency, Counting, and Frequency
points: `uniq` collapses only ADJACENT duplicate lines — this is the single most important fact about it, and why `sort | uniq` is the canonical pair
Because it only compares neighbors, uniq is O(n) with O(1) memory; the sort in front is what costs O(n log n)
`-c` prefixes each group with its count — `sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head` is the universal top-N frequency pipeline
`-d` prints only duplicated lines (one per group), `-D` prints every line of every duplicate group, `-u` prints only lines that appeared exactly once
`-i` case-insensitive comparison; `-f n` skips the first n fields; `-s n` skips the first n characters; `-w n` compares at most n characters
Field skipping enables 'dedupe by column': `sort -k2 | uniq -f1` treats the first field (a timestamp, say) as noise
`sort -u` vs `sort | uniq`: `sort -u` is faster (dedupes during the merge, less I/O) but cannot count. Use `uniq -c` when you need frequencies
`sort -u -k2,2` dedupes by key 2 and keeps an arbitrary representative line, while `uniq` compares the text after skipped fields — different semantics, easy to conflate
`uniq -c` output is right-aligned and space-padded, which breaks naive `cut -d' ' -f1`; pipe through `awk '{print $1}'` or `sed 's/^ *//'`
Order-preserving dedupe without sorting: `awk '!seen[$0]++'` — keeps first occurrence, O(n) time, O(distinct) memory
Counting without sorting: `awk '{c[$0]++} END{for(k in c) print c[k], k}'` — one pass, avoids the sort for huge inputs, but holds all distinct keys in RAM
Total distinct count shortcut: `sort -u file | wc -l`, or `awk '!seen[$0]++' file | wc -l` when input order matters

chapters.title: awk I: Records, Fields, and Program Structure
points: awk is a pattern-scanning language, not just a command: it splits input into RECORDS (lines) and each record into FIELDS, then runs `pattern { action }` rules against every record
`$0` is the whole record, `$1`..`$NF` the fields, `NF` = number of fields, `NR` = record number overall, `FNR` = record number within the current file
Default field splitting on runs of whitespace also strips leading/trailing blanks — this is why awk handles ragged `ls -l` output where cut fails
`-F` sets the field separator: `-F:` a char, `-F'\t'` a tab, `-F',[ ]*'` a REGEX (awk's FS is a regex when longer than one char), `-F''` splits into characters (gawk)
Special case: `FS=" "` (the default) means 'whitespace runs, trimmed'; `FS="[ ]"` means a single literal space, which does produce empty fields
`BEGIN{}` runs before any input (set FS, OFS, print headers); `END{}` runs after the last record (print totals). `awk 'BEGIN{...}'` with no input runs as a standalone calculator
A rule with a pattern and no action defaults to `{print}`; an action with no pattern runs on every record. `awk '/error/'` ≈ grep, `awk '{print $2}'` ≈ cut
Assigning to a field rebuilds `$0` using OFS: `awk '{$1=$1}1'` normalizes whitespace, and `awk -F, -v OFS='\t' '{$1=$1}1'` converts CSV to TSV
Output separators: `OFS` between print arguments, `ORS` after each record. `print a, b` uses OFS; `print a b` concatenates with nothing
`RS` sets the record separator — `RS=""` is paragraph mode (blank-line-separated records), `RS=";"` splits on semicolons; gawk allows a regex RS
Pass shell values in safely with `-v var=value` (available in BEGIN) or `var=value` between filenames (available after that file starts) — never interpolate shell variables into the program text
Field numbers are dynamic: `$NF` is the last field, `$(NF-1)` the second-to-last, and `$x` where x is a variable is legal — `awk -v c=3 '{print $c}'`

chapters.title: awk II: Patterns, Expressions, and Control Flow
points: Patterns can be: a regex `/error/`, an expression `$3 > 100`, a range `/start/,/end/`, `BEGIN`/`END`, or a combination with `&&`, `||`, `!`
Regex match operators: `$1 ~ /^a/` matches, `$1 !~ /^a/` does not match — the bare `/re/` form tests `$0`
Comparison is type-aware: awk keeps 'strnum' values, so `$1 == 10` compares numerically if field 1 looks numeric, but string-wise if it does not. Force with `$1+0` (number) or `$1""` (string)
Uninitialized variables are simultaneously `""` and `0`, which is why `sum += $3` needs no initialization and `if (!seen[x])` works
Control flow: `if/else`, `while`, `do..while`, `for(i=1;i<=NF;i++)`, `for(k in arr)`, plus `break`, `continue`, `next` (skip to next record), `nextfile`, `exit` (jumps to END)
`print` vs `printf`: `print` adds ORS and joins with OFS; `printf` gives format control and adds nothing — `printf "%-10s %6.2f\n", $1, $2`
Common format specifiers: `%s` string, `%d` integer, `%.2f` fixed decimal, `%5d` width, `%-5s` left align, `%%` literal percent
String functions: `length(s)`, `substr(s,i,n)` (1-indexed!), `index(s,t)`, `split(s,arr,sep)` (returns count), `toupper`/`tolower`, `sprintf`

`sub(re,rep)` replaces the first match, `gsub(re,rep)` all matches, both on `$0` unless a third target is given; both return the number of replacements. `&` in the replacement means the match, `\\&` a literal ampersand
`match(s,re)` sets `RSTART` and `RLENGTH`, letting you extract the matched substring: `match($0,/[0-9]+/); print substr($0,RSTART,RLENGTH)`

Redirect per-record output to files or commands: `print > "out_" $1 ".txt"` splits a file by column value; `print | "sort -n"` pipes out; close them with `close(name)` to avoid running out of descriptors
Math and misc: `int()`, `sqrt()`, `rand()`/`srand()`, `%` modulo, `^` exponent, and `system("cmd")` / `"cmd" | getline line` to call the shell

chapters.title: awk III: Arrays, Aggregation, and Real Programs
points: All awk arrays are associative — keys are strings, so `count["GET"]`, `count[$1]`, and `count[1]` are all the same mechanism
`arr[k]++` auto-creates the element with value 0 then increments: the whole idiom `!seen[$0]++` (print first occurrence only) rests on this
`k in arr` tests membership WITHOUT creating the key; `if (arr[k])` creates it as a side effect — a classic memory leak in long-running awk
`for (k in arr)` iterates in unspecified order; pipe to `sort`, or use gawk's `PROCINFO["sorted_in"]="@val_num_desc"`, when order matters
`delete arr[k]` removes one key, `delete arr` clears the array (gawk/POSIX 2018)
Multidimensional emulation: `arr[a,b]` joins the subscripts with `SUBSEP` (\034); split them back with `split(k, parts, SUBSEP)`
Group-and-sum, the canonical report: `awk '{sum[$1]+=$3} END{for(k in sum) print k, sum[k]}'`
Average, min, max in one pass: `awk '{s+=$1; n++; if(n==1||$1<mn)mn=$1; if($1>mx)mx=$1} END{print mn, mx, s/n}'` — guard `n>0` in END or you divide by zero on empty input
Two-file join idiom: `awk 'NR==FNR{map[$1]=$2; next} $1 in map {print $0, map[$1]}' lookup.txt data.txt` — `NR==FNR` is true only while reading the first file
Column reordering and computed columns, which cut cannot do: `awk -F, -v OFS=, '{print $3, $1, $2*1.08}'`
User functions: `function f(a, b,   tmp) { ... }` — parameters after the extra spaces are the convention for locals, since all other variables are global

Implementations differ: `mawk` is fastest but limited, `gawk` adds `gensub()`, true regex RS, `asort()`, `strftime()`, bignum; `busybox awk` is minimal. Write POSIX awk for portability, reach for gawk features knowingly

chapters.title: Building Pipelines: Composition Patterns
points: Canonical shape: extract → filter → transform → aggregate → order → limit, e.g. `cut -d' ' -f1 access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -20`
Top talkers by IP: `awk '{print $1}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head`
Error rate by hour: `awk '$9>=500 {split($4,t,":"); print t[2]}' access.log | sort | uniq -c`
Largest directories: `du -sh */ | sort -h | tail`; disk usage over a threshold: `du -m . | awk '$1>100'`
Word frequency: `tr -cs '[:alpha:]' '\n' < book.txt | tr 'A-Z' 'a-z' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head`
Set operations on sorted files with `comm`: `comm -12 a b` (intersection), `comm -23 a b` (a minus b), `comm -3` (symmetric difference) — inputs MUST be sorted the same way
Filter early, sort late: every line you drop before `sort` is a line it never has to buffer or compare
Collapse stages when one tool does it all: `grep pat | awk '{print $2}'` → `awk '/pat/{print $2}'`; `cat f | grep x` → `grep x f` (the useless-use-of-cat)
Use `xargs` to feed a pipeline into a command: `grep -rlZ 'old' . | xargs -0 -P4 sed -i 's/old/new/g'` — `-P` parallelizes, `-0` survives odd filenames
Debug a long pipeline by bisecting: append `| head -5` after each stage, or insert `| tee /tmp/stageN |` to snapshot intermediate output
Pipeline exit status is the LAST command's by default; `set -o pipefail` makes any failing stage fail the pipeline, and `${PIPESTATUS[@]}` inspects each
`process substitution` breaks the linear shape when you need two streams: `diff <(sort a) <(sort b)`, `comm -12 <(cut -f1 a|sort) <(cut -f1 b|sort)`

chapters.title: Trade-offs: Which Tool, and What It Costs
points: Capability ladder: grep = select lines; cut = slice fixed columns; sed = per-line edit; awk = fields + variables + arithmetic + state; then Perl/Python for structured formats
Rule of thumb: use the least powerful tool that solves it — smaller startup cost, faster, and less to get wrong
Speed (typical, ASCII, per GB): `cut`/`tr` fastest, `grep -F` next, `grep` ERE, `mawk`, `sed`, `gawk`, then `grep -P`, then a Python script — often a 10–50x span end to end
Memory: grep/sed/cut/awk-without-arrays are O(1) in input size; `sort` is O(n) (spilling to disk); awk with arrays is O(distinct keys)
Latency: `sort` and `awk END{}` are blocking — nothing comes out until the input ends, so they cannot be used mid-stream on `tail -f`
`LC_ALL=C` is the single biggest free speedup: it disables UTF-8 collation and multibyte decoding for grep, sort, and awk. Only safe when your data is ASCII or byte order is acceptable
Parallelism: pipelines already use one core per stage; `sort --parallel`, `xargs -P`, and GNU `parallel --pipe` scale further, but reordering output is the cost
`grep | wc -l` vs `grep -c`: the latter avoids a process and a stream copy, and matters in tight loops

Regex engine trade-off: POSIX grep/sed use a DFA — linear time, no backtracking blowup, but no lookaround or backreferences. PCRE gives power at the risk of catastrophic backtracking on inputs like `(a+)+b`
Portability trade-off: GNU extensions (`\b`, `sed -i` without a suffix, `grep -P`, `sort -h`) fail on BSD/macOS/busybox. POSIX-only scripts are uglier but run everywhere
Know when to stop: real CSV with quoted commas, JSON, XML, or multi-line records are NOT line-oriented — reach for `jq`, `csvkit`, `xmlstarlet`, or Python instead of writing an unmaintainable sed
Maintainability: a 5-stage pipeline someone can read beats a single clever awk one-liner nobody can modify — and a 15-line awk program with comments beats both

chapters.title: Common Mistakes and Silent Corruptions
points: Double quotes around patterns let the shell expand `$`, `` ` ``, `!`, and `\` first — always single-quote regexes and awk programs
BRE/ERE confusion: `grep 'foo(bar)'` looks for a literal parenthesis; `grep -E` or `\(` is needed. Symmetrically, `grep -E 'a\+'` matches a literal plus
Unescaped `.` matches any character: `grep '192.168.1.1'` also matches `192a168b1c1`. Escape it or use `grep -F`
`sort | uniq` forgotten: `uniq` alone silently reports only adjacent duplicates and undercounts, with no error
`sort -k2` means field 2 through end of line, not field 2 — always write `-k2,2`
`cut -d' '` on aligned or multi-space output yields empty fields; use awk's default whitespace splitting instead
`sed -i` with no backup on a failed regex destroys the file; test without `-i` first, or use `-i.bak`
Special characters in a sed replacement: `&`, `\`, and the delimiter must be escaped, or the substitution silently produces wrong text
CRLF line endings make `$` anchors and numeric comparisons fail invisibly (`grep 'foo$'` misses `foo\r`); fix with `tr -d '\r'` or `dos2unix` up front
Locale surprises: `[a-z]` in a UTF-8 locale can match accented or uppercase characters via collation; use `[[:lower:]]` or `LC_ALL=C`
Filenames with spaces/newlines break `for f in $(grep -l ...)`; use `-Z` with `xargs -0`, or `while IFS= read -r -d ''`
`grep pat file | wc -l` counts lines, `grep -o pat file | wc -l` counts occurrences — reporting the wrong one is a common analysis error
Redirecting to the input file (`sort f > f`) truncates it to empty before sort ever reads it
`awk '$1 == "0010"'` fails when awk treats the field as the number 10 — the strnum rule. Force a string compare with `$1"" == "0010"`

chapters.title: Summary: The Whole Toolchain on One Page
points: grep = select lines by pattern. Key flags: `-i -v -w -o -c -n -r -E -F -P -q -A/-B/-C --include`
sed = per-line edit via the read/execute/auto-print cycle. Key form: `[addr]s/re/rep/gpi`, plus `-n p`, `d`, `-i.bak`, `-E`, and the hold space for multi-line work
awk = field-aware mini-language. Key form: `BEGIN{} /pat/{action} END{}` with `$1..$NF, NF, NR, FNR, FS, OFS, RS`, associative arrays, and printf
cut = fast fixed-delimiter column slicing, single-char delimiter, file order only. tr = character translate/delete/squeeze
sort = ordering with `-n -h -V -u -r -s -t -kN,N`; the memory and latency wall. uniq = adjacency-only collapsing with `-c -d -u -f -w`
The three canonical pipelines: `sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head` (top N), `awk '!seen[$0]++'` (order-preserving dedupe), `awk '{s[$1]+=$2} END{for(k in s) print k, s[k]}'` (group-by-sum)
Escalation path: grep → cut → sed → awk → Python. Stop at the first tool that does the job cleanly
Correctness checklist: single-quote patterns, escape dots, `-k2,2` not `-k2`, sort before uniq, strip CRLF, set `LC_ALL=C` when you want byte semantics
Performance checklist: filter before sort, prefer `-F` over regex, merge adjacent grep/cut into one awk, use `LC_ALL=C`, and parallelize with `xargs -P` only after measuring
Portability checklist: assume POSIX BRE/ERE, avoid `\b \d \K sed -i` bare, `sort -h`, and `grep -P` in scripts that must run on macOS or busybox
Exit codes are part of the interface: 0/1/2 from grep drives `if`, `&&`, and CI gates — and `set -o pipefail` is what makes a multi-stage pipeline fail honestly
Everything above is one idea repeated: text is lines, lines are fields, and small composable filters connected by pipes beat one large program
